title: Teaching
text:
Teaching Philosophy
I view mathematics and statistics as disciplines that are best learned through a combination of conceptual understanding, structured problem solving, and practical application.
In teaching, I aim to help students move beyond memorizing formulas or procedures and instead understand:

Why a method works
When it should be used
What assumptions it relies on
How to interpret results
How to communicate reasoning clearly

I also believe students learn quantitative material best when they are encouraged to ask questions, work through examples, and connect abstract ideas to concrete problems.

title: Projects
text:
A selection of projects demonstrating my experience in statistical modeling, machine learning, spatial analysis, public health analytics, large language models, and reproducible research.



Medical Specialty Classification from Clinical Conversations

Python GPT-2 NLP Gradio

Fine-tuned GPT-2 Medium on 13,492 clinical conversations using a two-block parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy.
Highlights

79.1% test accuracy
0.799 macro-F1
25.2M trainable parameters
Four medical specialties: Cardiology, Neurology, Orthopedics, and General Medicine
t-SNE embedding analysis
Interactive Gradio deployment


View GitHub View Report




Spatial Statistics, Machine Learning, and Public Health

R Spatial Statistics XGBoost SHAP

Analyzed lung cancer mortality across 2,536 U.S. counties using CDC Social Vulnerability Index, CDC PLACES, and National Cancer Institute data.
Methods

Robust OLS and quantile regression
Global Moran’s I and LISA
Spatial error models
Random Forest and XGBoost with SHAP interpretation
Mediation analysis

Key Results

232 unexplained high-mortality spatial clusters identified
COPD mediated approximately 50.8% of the county-level smoking–mortality association


View Report




County-Level Public Health Analysis

R Spatial Analysis Regression Mapping

Analyzed 2,299 U.S. counties to examine the relationship between food insecurity and chronic disease burden.
Methods

Standardized chronic disease burden index
Multivariable regression
Sensitivity analysis
Spatial autocorrelation
Geographic mapping

Key Results

Identified 408 counties with jointly high food insecurity and chronic disease burden
Significant spatial clustering was observed across the United States


View Report




Gender-Based Comparative Statistical Analysis

Minitab Logistic Regression ROC Analysis Public Health

Analyzed cardiovascular disease risk factors in a public dataset of 68,672 adults, with emphasis on whether associations differed between women and men.
Methods

Spearman correlation
Welch’s two-sample t test and Kruskal–Wallis tests
Chi-square test of independence
Binary logistic regression with gender-specific models
ROC and AUC analysis

Key Results

Combined logistic model achieved an AUC of approximately 0.791
Age, BMI, blood pressure, and cholesterol were important predictors
Gender-specific models showed similar risk structures with differences in coefficient magnitude


View Report




CDC BRFSS Analysis

SAS R Regression ANOVA

Analyzed 253,680 CDC BRFSS observations to investigate clinical, behavioral, demographic, and socioeconomic factors associated with diabetes-related outcomes.
Methods

Chi-square tests and factorial ANOVA
Multiple and logistic regression
Model selection and diagnostics
Sex-stratified analysis




Socioeconomic and Health Indicators

R Regression Predictive Modeling

Built a multiple linear regression model to predict life expectancy across African countries using socioeconomic and health indicators.
Key Results

Final model achieved an adjusted R² of approximately 0.98
Adult mortality and HIV incidence emerged as major predictors




Malaria Among Pregnant Women in Ghana

Machine Learning KNN Public Health

Applied explainable machine learning methods to Demographic and Health Survey data to predict malaria risk among pregnant women.
Key Results

K-Nearest Neighbors achieved the strongest performance, with an AUC of approximately 0.88
Age and anaemia status ranked among the most important predictors




Malaria Risk Among Children Under Five in Ghana

Machine Learning Random Forest Neural Networks

Used the 2019 Ghana Malaria Indicator Survey to evaluate machine learning models for identifying risk factors associated with malaria incidence among children under five.

Python NumPy Linear Algebra

Developed a Python program that generated fractal patterns by repeatedly applying affine transformations using matrix operations and translation vectors.

title: Samuel Bonney
text:
About Me
Hi, I’m Samuel Bonney 👋
I’m a graduate student in Applied Statistics at Illinois State University, where I spend most of my time asking a deceptively simple question: how well does a model actually fit the data?
My research focuses on nonparametric statistical methodology, specifically tilted kernel density estimation and Bickel–Rosenblatt goodness-of-fit testing. I like working on methods that make fewer assumptions about the world and still deliver reliable answers, and I test them the hard way, through simulation studies.
Beyond my thesis, I apply statistics to problems that matter for public health: mapping lung cancer mortality and chronic disease burden across U.S. counties, using explainable machine learning to understand malaria risk in Ghana, and fine-tuning large language models to classify clinical conversations. Before coming to Illinois State, I earned my B.A. in Mathematics and Statistics from the University of Ghana.
What ties all of this together is that I enjoy the full journey: the theory, the code, the simulations, and finally turning the results into something people can actually understand.
Away from the data, you’ll probably find me at a pool table or a table tennis table. Both are, if you think about it, applied geometry and probability with a lot more trash talk. I also enjoy video games in my downtime, which I tell myself counts as research into decision-making under uncertainty.

title: Research
text:
Graduate Thesis

Nonparametric Tilted Density Estimation and Bickel–Rosenblatt Goodness-of-Fit Testing
My graduate thesis investigates tilted kernel density estimators and their use in goodness-of-fit testing.
The project focuses on selecting bandwidth and probability weights using cross-validation-based procedures and evaluating the resulting estimators through extensive simulation studies.
The work examines:

Tilted kernel density estimation
Cross-validation-based bandwidth and probability-weight selection
Bickel–Rosenblatt goodness-of-fit testing
Asymptotic behavior
Empirical test size and statistical power
Comparison with conventional kernel density estimators

The broader goal is to understand whether tilted density estimators can improve inferential performance relative to conventional kernel-based approaches under different data-generating settings.

title: Research
text:
Research Areas
My applied work falls into three main areas. Full methods, results, and reports for each project are on the Projects page.

Spatial Epidemiology and Public Health
I study geographic variation in health outcomes across U.S. counties by combining regression, spatial statistics, and machine learning. My work on lung cancer mortality identified unexplained high-mortality clusters after accounting for socioeconomic and behavioral factors and found that COPD mediated about half of the smoking–mortality association. A related project on food insecurity and chronic disease identified counties facing both burdens at once, highlighting priority areas for intervention.


Machine Learning for Health in Ghana
My earlier research used explainable machine learning to study malaria risk in Ghana, including prediction of malaria among pregnant women from Demographic and Health Survey data, and my undergraduate thesis on risk factors for malaria among children under five using the 2019 Ghana Malaria Indicator Survey.


Large Language Models for Clinical Text
In BioMed-Scribe, I adapted GPT-2 Medium to classify clinical conversations into medical specialties using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, showing how large language models can be specialized for clinical tasks while limiting the number of trainable parameters.

title: Research
text:
Current Research Direction
My current work is increasingly focused on nonparametric statistical methodology, simulation-based inference, and the integration of classical statistical techniques with modern machine learning methods. I am especially interested in research that is methodologically rigorous, computationally reproducible, and applicable to meaningful scientific and public-health questions.
